entry.title: Learning Joint Graphical Model with Computational Efficiency, Dynamic Regularization, and Adaptation

link.title: Learning Joint Graphical Model with Computational Efficiency, Dynamic Regularization, and Adaptation

entry.content:
Multi-sourced datasets are common in studies of variable interactions, for example, heterogeneous gene networks, cross-domain recommendation, etc., where each source induces a related but distinct dependency structure. Joint learning of multiple graphical models (i.e., multiple precision matrices) has emerged as an important tool in analyzing such data. Unlike separate learning, joint learning can leverage shared structural patterns across graphs to yield more accurate results. In this paper, we present an adaptive method named MIGHT (Multi-task Iterative Graphical Hard Thresholding) to estimate multiple graphs jointly. We introduce an $\ell_0$-based similarity measure, reformulate the joint model as a series of multi-task learning problems, and solve them using a dynamically regularized algorithm based on iterative hard thresholding. By leveraging the efficiency of the iterative procedure and the inherent parallelizability of the nodewise framework, the proposed method is computationally efficient and amenable to parallel implementation. Theoretically, we derive the non-asymptotic error bound for the resulting estimator under joint Gaussian graphical models. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is adaptive to heterogeneous column-wise signal strengths: for nodes with strong signals, our estimator achieves improved error bounds and selection consistency adaptively, and also exhibits asymptotic normality without an additional debiasing step. The performance of our method is illustrated through numerical simulations and real-data analysis on a cancer gene-expression RNA-seq dataset.

entry.title: Learning smooth dynamics via Kinematic Interpolants

link.title: Learning smooth dynamics via Kinematic Interpolants

entry.content:
Inferring dynamics from real-world experimental data is inherently ambiguous, as many plausible dynamical systems can explain the same positional observations at measurement times. For higher fidelity modeling of applications ranging from single-cell RNA to vortex dynamics and even flocking of birds, scientific observables increasingly also include velocity estimates that serve to resolve this issue. However, incorporating this rich information in a scalable manner, free of simulation or unnecessary approximations, has remained a difficult challenge. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Interpolants (KI), a novel framework that extends the seminal methodology of stochastic interpolants to infer nonlinear dynamics across multiple snapshots in phase space, i.e., observables with position and velocity measurements. Empirically, we demonstrate that across several scientific datasets, KI achieves superior reconstruction of the underlying dynamics compared to existing baselines while requiring only a fraction of the training time.

entry.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere

link.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere

entry.content:
Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

entry.title: Marginal generalized raking with parametric working models

link.title: Marginal generalized raking with parametric working models

entry.content:
Generalized raking (GR) was originally developed in the survey statistics literature to incorporate auxiliary information in estimation. Recently, it has been used in the biostatistical and epidemiological literature to estimate regression coefficients in parametric models in cases with missing data, including missing data by design (e.g., two-phase studies). In the regression parameter context, the optimal GR estimator has been shown to be equivalent to the optimal augmented inverse probability weighted estimator. In this paper, we generalize the influence function-based theory for GR to marginal estimands; we call our approach marginal generalized raking. We contrast our approach to a procedure that marginalizes a conditional GR estimator of regression parameters; while the former approach is doubly robust, i.e. is consistent if either the missing-data model or the optimal raking variable is estimated consistently, our proposed approach is multiply robust, allowing either the outcome regression or treatment propensity score to also be misspecified. We compare the approaches in both fully-synthetic simulations and in an application using data from an observational cohort of persons living with HIV.

entry.title: Measuring Differences between Conditional Distributions using Kernel Embeddings

link.title: Measuring Differences between Conditional Distributions using Kernel Embeddings

entry.content:
Comparing conditional distributions is a fundamental challenge in statistics and machine learning, with applications across a wide range of domains. While proposed methods for measuring discrepancies using kernel embeddings of distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) provide powerful non-parametric techniques, the existing literature remains fragmented and lacks a unified theoretical treatment. This paper addresses this gap by establishing a coherent framework for studying kernel-based methods to measure divergence between conditional distributions through what we refer to as conditional maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD). The CMMD consists of a family of metrics which we call levels, with three special cases each using a different type of RKHS embedding: CMMD$_0$ (conditional mean operators), CMMD$_1$ (conditional mean embeddings), and CMMD$_2$ (joint mean embeddings). We additionally introduce a general level $s$ CMMD, clarifying the required assumptions, and establishing mathematical connections between the levels through the lens of operator-based smoothing. In addition to reviewing previously proposed estimators, we introduce a novel doubly robust estimator for the CMMD that maintains consistency provided the product of errors of the underlying models reduces sufficiently fast. We provide numerical experiments demonstrating that the CMMD effectively captures complex conditional dependencies for statistical testing.

entry.title: Measuring frailty in older adults: an indicator based on a super-classifier

link.title: Measuring frailty in older adults: an indicator based on a super-classifier

entry.content:
Identifying frail older adults in an ageing population is essential for improving healthcare services. This study proposes a composite indicator to assess individual frailty levels using administrative healthcare data. Given the complex and multidimensional nature of frailty, a multi-outcome approach is adopted. Following an extensive literature review, a set of adverse health events is selected as proxies for frailty. These events were modelled using logistic classifiers, with frailty determinants (associated to adverse health events, selected using a gradient tree boosting) serving as covariates. The sensitivity and specificity of each classifier is used to compose their combined likelihood. From this, we derive an indicator capable of quantifying frailty across the population. The indicator shows robust performance across multiple outcomes and over time. Its primary innovation lies in allowing the use of diverse and outcome-specific sets of frailty determinants without any structural constraint. Overall, we offer an effective tool for quantifying frailty among older adults, potentially supporting health authorities in the prevention of frailty-related adverse events.

entry.title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks

link.title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks

entry.content:
Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function’s linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.

entry.title: Minimax-optimal Scaling Laws in Ridge Regression via Transfer Learning

link.title: Minimax-optimal Scaling Laws in Ridge Regression via Transfer Learning

entry.content:
Pretrained models are often reused across downstream tasks, motivating the question of whether this transfer learning procedure can provide a substantial performance improvement, namely, in terms of the scaling law. We address this question in the prototypical setting of high-dimensional regression, where (i) a pretrained \emph{source} model is trained via ridge regression, and (ii) a fine-tuned \emph{target} model is regularized via the $L_2$ distance from the source estimator. First, we establish a deterministic equivalent for the risk of this two-step procedure under both model and covariance shift. Next, by specializing the deterministic equivalent to a shared regression function and commuting power-law covariance spectra, we identify a regime where the resulting scaling law achieves the minimax-optimal exponent. Notably, in this regime, the optimal source regularization depends on source data only, indicating its universality across all targets. Furthermore, we show that the same optimal rate is achieved by performing the fine-tuning step via one-pass stochastic gradient descent. We support our theoretical analysis via experiments on both synthetic settings and language models.

link.title: Missing value imputation with adversarial random forests - MissARF

entry.content:
Handling missing values is a common challenge in biostatistical analyses, typically addressed by imputation methods. We propose a novel, fast, and easy-to-use imputation method called missing value imputation with adversarial random forests (MissARF), based on generative machine learning, that provides both single and multiple imputation. MissARF employs adversarial random forest (ARF) for density estimation and data synthesis. To impute a missing value of an observation, we condition on the non-missing values and sample from the estimated conditional distribution generated by ARF. Our experiments demonstrate that MissARF performs comparably to state-of-the-art single and multiple imputation methods in terms of imputation quality and fast runtime with no additional costs for multiple imputation.

entry.title: Multiple testing in multi-stream sequential change detection

link.title: Multiple testing in multi-stream sequential change detection

entry.content:
Multi-stream sequential change detection involves simultaneously monitoring many data streams and raising an alarm when their distributions change. We study the multiple testing issues that arise naturally in this setting. We first point out a fundamental tension between the criteria used in change detection and multiple testing: any procedure with finite average run length (ARL) must have worst-case false discovery rate (FDR) and family-wise error rate equal to one. Given this conflict, we find a middle ground by introducing the error over patience (EOP) class of Type I error metrics, which measure error relative to expected monitoring time. To control the EOP, we propose procedures combining e-detectors, which generalize Shiryaev-Roberts and CUSUM methods, with the recent e-Benjamini-Hochberg and e-Bonferroni methods for multiple testing. Our EOP guarantees hold uniformly over changepoints and stopping times with finite expectation, allowing dependence when each e-detector remains valid using information from all streams. If finite ARL is forfeited, using e-processes instead yields ordinary FDR and per-family error control at stopping times. We also prove power and delay bounds for Gaussian changes, establish first-order minimax optimality, and compare our procedures with existing methods in numerical experiments.

link.title: Negative-binomial ensemble filtering for discrete-time Hawkes network reconstruction

entry.content:
We develop a sequential ensemble filter for reconstructing directed excitation networks from overdispersed multivariate counts observed on a regular time grid. The data-generating model is a discrete-time negative-binomial Hawkes process, for which we prove exact first- and second-moment stability conditions and derive a row-wise sufficient condition. The filter learns the network and the dispersion online, and a row-composition parameter forecast keeps enough ensemble variation to respond to structural change. In synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that a Poisson-based filter provides comparable point-estimate accuracy of the network, while the proposed filter provides substantially better calibrated predictive and parameter uncertainty. Under an abrupt redistribution of influence, the filter recovers connections that are absent before the change. An application to daily property-crime counts in sixteen Chicago community areas gives broadly calibrated one-step predictions and a recovered network consistent with independent temporal and geographic information.

entry.title: No-Regret Language Generation

link.title: No-Regret Language Generation

entry.content:
We introduce no-regret generation, which requires a generator to make a sublinear number of mistakes uniformly over all demonstration sequences and compatible target languages. We also formulate an agnostic variant that allows arbitrary demonstrations that may not be compatible with any languages. For both settings, we introduce tree-based mistake-forcing dimensions that exactly characterize finite-horizon minimax complexity and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for no-regret generation. Our characterizations reveal a rich spectrum of generation rates: up to constant rescaling, every admissible nondecreasing profile is attainable in both the realizable and agnostic settings. Finally, we connect generation complexity to online prediction: for language classes of finite Littlestone dimension (d), we obtain realizable mistake bounds of (O(d\log(1+T/d))) and agnostic regret bounds of (O(\sqrt{dT\log(1+T/d)})). The realizable bound is optimal up to universal constants.

entry.title: Online Inference for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Online Inference for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
In this paper, we study online statistical inference for quantile-based distributional policy evaluation, which aims to characterize the distribution of discounted cumulative rewards under a given policy. To obtain a finite-dimensional representation of the return distribution, we consider the fixed point $\bm\eta_m$ of the quantile-projected distributional Bellman equation, parameterized by the quantile vector $\bm\theta_m$. We develop two online inference procedures for $\bm\theta_m$, covering synchronous and asynchronous sampling from a generative model as well as Markovian data. The first method uses the trajectory of quantile temporal-difference learning (QTD). We establish functional central limit theorems for the partial sums of QTD iterates and construct a recursively computable random-scaling statistic. The resulting confidence intervals have asymptotically exact coverage at deterministic horizons, with length of order $T^{-1/2}$ in probability. The second method constructs anytime-valid confidence intervals directly from samples. Exploiting the monotonicity of the quantile Bellman map, we develop a computationally explicit coordinate-shaving algorithm with finite-sample simultaneous coverage. Under positive limiting state-visit frequencies, the resulting confidence intervals have lengths of order $\sqrt{\log\log T/T}$, which we establish as classwise optimal through a matching lower bound. Together, these results provide complementary guarantees for online inference in quantile distributional reinforcement learning, combining asymptotically exact fixed-horizon inference with finite-sample anytime validity.

entry.title: On the Sample Complexity of Active Learning with Membership Queries

link.title: On the Sample Complexity of Active Learning with Membership Queries

entry.content:
This work revisits a fundamental question in active learning: how powerful is the ability to synthesize arbitrary queries? Compared to pool-based active learning, where the learner only selects queries from a given unlabeled pool, it has been observed that this seemingly mild change in query ability may dramatically alter the difficulty of statistical learning. In particular some hypothesis classes, such as two dimensional halfspaces, permit only polynomial error decay in the number of samples when the learner must draw its labels from the pool, yet become exponentially learnable once synthesized queries are allowed. This striking gap suggests that membership query synthesis induces a fundamentally different mode of learning, one that is not adequately captured by existing active learning theory and calls for new analytical tools to characterize its sample complexity for general hypothesis classes. Motivated by this phenomenon, we develop several sufficient conditions, present intriguing examples, and propose a conjectural perspective toward understanding which hypothesis classes admit efficient learning through synthesized queries.

entry.title: On the Trade-off Between Information Loss and Generalization in Sparse Attention

link.title: On the Trade-off Between Information Loss and Generalization in Sparse Attention

entry.content:
To mitigate the quadratic complexity bottleneck of the Transformer, sparse attention has emerged as a pivotal technology. Despite the extensive empirical success of sparse Transformers, the theoretical understanding of sparse attention remains fragmented. In particular, two fundamental questions remain unclear: (1) How does sparsification affect the information fidelity of attention mechanisms? (2) How does this information loss interact with the generalization behavior of the model? To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a systematic analysis of the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence and of the generalization gap of sparse attention mechanisms. Specifically, we first characterize the approximation error via the JS divergence. Through an order-statistics-based concentration analysis of the truncation mass alpha — where the attention scores are assumed to be independent and identically distributed sub-Gaussian random variables with parameter sigma — the JS divergence between the full attention distribution and the sparse attention distribution is shown to admit the closed form log 2 + ((1 - alpha)/2) log(1 - alpha) - ((2 - alpha)/2) log(2 - alpha). Subsequently, we derive a generalization bound through Rademacher complexity, quantified by O(gamma * sqrt(M/n) * (sqrt(log(3eL/M)) + sqrt(pi)/2)). Furthermore, building on a mutual-information-based generalization bound together with an entropy and covering-number analysis of the sparse hypothesis class, we obtain the sparsity-dependent generalization bound O(sqrt((M/(2n)) * (log(eL/M) + log(1 + 2/epsilon)))). Our analysis shows that sparsity reduces the complexity of the considered hypothesis class while introducing approximation error that can be quantified by the JS divergence. These findings provide a theoretical characterization of the trade-off between information fidelity and generalization in sparse Transformer architectures.

entry.title: On the foundations of anthropic reasoning: Implications for life across the universe

link.title: On the foundations of anthropic reasoning: Implications for life across the universe

entry.content:
With only one confirmed example, namely the Earth, the abundance of life across the universe remains deeply uncertain, and local evidence about Earth’s particular circumstances can significantly shape our knowledge of life elsewhere. Such extrapolation is difficult not only because of this sample size of one, but also due to observer selection effects discussed under the Anthropic Principle. In this paper, we describe and apply a framework called Full Indexical Conditioning (FIC) for performing Bayesian inference in this situation. Inspired by, but distinct from, Full Non-Indexical Conditioning, FIC conditions on all evidence available to the reasoner while considering that this evidence could have been otherwise. We address the reference class problem associated with such reasoning, demonstrating that substantive conclusions are unaffected by the choice of reference class provided it is sufficiently large. We apply FIC to several problems in astrobiology, including the Doomsday argument, the early abiogenesis time, and our location around a G-type rather than M-type star, clarifying the foundations of these arguments. We conclude that the early abiogenesis time does not rule out pessimistic possibilities for life’s abundance, and that while life around M stars may be uncommon, its temporal distribution could extend far into the future. Ultimately, FIC offers a clear conceptual framework, grounded in straightforward probability theory, for tackling problems involving anthropic selection effects.

entry.title: Optimal approximation of smooth functions by ReLU neural networks

link.title: Optimal approximation of smooth functions by ReLU neural networks

entry.content:
We study uniform approximation of the H"older ball $\mathcal H_1^s([0,1]^D)$ by fully connected ReLU networks. Except in the one-dimensional Lipschitz case, existing constructions remain separated from the information-theoretic efficiency limit. This article closes the gap for every $s>0$ and $D\ge1$: networks with width $O(N)$, depth $O(L)$, and parameter magnitude $O(1)$ attain uniform approximation error of order $(N^2L^2\log N)^{-s/D}$. No relation between width and depth is required. The construction uses new encoding and decoding mechanisms that exploit higher-order finite-difference bounds for local Taylor coefficients of the target function. As a statistical consequence, empirical risk minimizers over the corresponding clipped network classes attain the minimax regression rate $n^{-2s/(2s+D)}$ without additional logarithmic factors. The paper also gives a detailed exposition of the key approximation techniques, covering both established and new mechanisms.

entry.title: Optimal estimates for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of deep random ReLU neural networks

link.title: Optimal estimates for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of deep random ReLU neural networks

entry.content:
This paper studies the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of ReLU neural networks $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ with random parameters for $p \in [1,\infty]$. The distribution of the weights follows a variant of the He initialization. In the case of zero-bias networks, we derive matching high-probability upper and lower bounds for wide networks that differ at most by an absolute constant. The bounds reveal two remarkable phenomena. First, the bounds grow root-logarithmically in terms of the depth of the net. Second, the behavior of the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants varies significantly between the regimes $p \in [1,2)$ and $p \in [2,\infty]$. For $p \in [2,\infty]$, the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constant behaves similarly to $|g|_{p’}$, where $g \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a standard Gaussian vector and $1/p + 1/p’ = 1$. In contrast, for $p \in [1,2)$, the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constant aligns more closely with $|g|_2$. For networks with possibly nonzero biases, we obtain the same lower bounds without assumptions on the bias distributions. For symmetric bias distributions with bounded densities, we also derive high-probability upper bounds for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants. For fixed sub-exponential bias distributions, these upper bounds differ from the lower bounds by a factor that has square-root dependence on the depth and logarithmic dependence on the width.

entry.title: Optimal subsampling approach for Cox models under large-scale length-biased right-censored data

link.title: Optimal subsampling approach for Cox models under large-scale length-biased right-censored data

entry.content:
With the rapid advancement of data acquisition technologies, massive survival data have become increasingly prevalent, posing substantial computational challenges for the standard Cox proportional hazards model under complex censoring and truncation mechanisms. This paper addresses the analysis of large-scale length-biased right-censored data within the Cox model framework. We propose a novel subsampling approach to enhance computational efficiency for large samples and establish theoretically that the resulting subsample estimator provides an efficient approximation to the full-data estimator, while preserving consistency and asymptotic normality. Explicit optimal subsampling probabilities are derived under A- and L-optimality criteria. To facilitate practical implementation, we develop an efficient two-step estimation algorithm. Extensive numerical simulations and an empirical analysis of U.S. airline flight operation data evaluate the estimation performance and computational gains under various censoring rates and sample sizes. The results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces computational cost while preserving statistical accuracy, offering a practical and scalable solution for analyzing large-scale length-biased right-censored survival data.

entry.title: Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs

link.title: Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs

entry.content:
Primal-dual methods for constrained Markov decision processes are analyzed under a two-timescale assumption, with non-stationarity entering through two channels. In the additive channel, where the constraint level oscillates, the dual oscillation saturates at a floor set by the moving optimum and is amplified linearly by the timescale ratio. In the parametric channel, where the constraint sensitivity oscillates, a coherent modulation carries no resonant forcing at any depth: the dual update’s stiffness modulation cancels the primal update’s damping modulation. Instability instead comes from a mismatch between the constraint estimate used by the primal update and the measurement used by the dual update, producing a parametric resonance at twice the pair’s natural frequency. The tolerated mismatch grows with the square root of the forcing bandwidth and collapses with the square root of the dual-to-primal step-size ratio. These results hold on the tangent linear-quadratic reduction around an active saddle, for one constraint and for $K$ constraints under a common modulation and an isotropy condition. Driving both updates from the same estimate removes the resonant forcing but introduces a stationary offset equal to the estimator’s bias. In a Lagrangian soft actor-critic agent, the multiplier locks onto the sub-harmonic at the timescale ratios its identified linear loop predicts and a coherent cost critic suppresses the lock-in, while a proportional (PID) term, predicted to leave the lock-in in place, suppresses most of it through the projection of the multiplier.

link.title: Pattern Graph Models for Non-monotone Missing Data with an Application to Myocardial Infarction Complications

entry.content:
Non-monotone missingness is frequently encountered in practice, with intermittent dropout and re-entry in longitudinal studies as a canonical example. Under non-monotone missingness, the missing at random (MAR) assumption often lacks a clear causal interpretation and imposes implicit constraints on the joint distribution that may be difficult to justify. Within the pattern graph framework, we propose a fully parametric estimation procedure that combines pattern-graph-identified response probabilities with a parametric outcome model through an EM algorithm with fractional imputation. Under correct model specification and explicit regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality when the fractional imputation is exact or sufficiently accurate, and, under additional moment conditions, justify parametric bootstrap variance estimation. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed approach is competitive across a range of settings and provides substantial efficiency gains for joint probability estimation when fully observed cases are scarce. The methods are illustrated through an analysis of mortality risk factors in data on myocardial infarction complications.

entry.title: Proximal Causal Inference for Time Series from N-of-1Mobile Device Data

link.title: Proximal Causal Inference for Time Series from N-of-1Mobile Device Data

entry.content:
Unmeasured confounding challenges causal inference in intensive longitudinal studies, potentially biasing treatment effect estimates. The proximal causal inference (PCI) framework offers a promising approach to identification using proxies or negative control variables in the presence of hidden confounding bias. While prior literature considers the joint effect of time-varying treatments, our work extends the framework to a time series setting to estimate the contemporaneous or lagged effect of time-varying treatments. We demonstrate that under traditional PCI assumptions, we can recover unbiased effect estimation in the presence of unmeasured confounding by leveraging the intensive longitudinal nature of time series data. Specifically, we develop identifiability conditions and show that past and future observations can be employed as natural proxies for unmeasured confounders. We further develop the bridge function required for valid PCI estimation along with asymptotic variance. Simulation studies illustrate our method’s validity and robustness to violation of certain PCI identification assumptions. We demonstrate the potential for studying socio-environmental exposure health effects by applying our method to a smartphone study of bipolar patients. Our work contributes to the growing literature on PCI and provides a powerful tool for analyzing longitudinal data, including in observational mobile health research prone to confounding bias.

entry.title: RAW-Explainer: Post-hoc Explanations of Path Reasoning Graph Neural Networks for Knowledge Graph Completion

link.title: RAW-Explainer: Post-hoc Explanations of Path Reasoning Graph Neural Networks for Knowledge Graph Completion

entry.content:
Path reasoning graph neural networks have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on knowledge graph completion tasks such as link prediction. However, interpreting their predictions remains a challenging open problem, as most GNN explainability methods target node-level or graph-level tasks. In this paper, we propose RAW-Explainer ($\underline{Ra}$ndom $\underline{W}$alk Explainer), a novel explainability method tailored to path reasoning GNNs that generates connected, concise, and interpretable subgraph explanations for link prediction in knowledge graphs. Our method uses heterogeneous information to identify factual explanations and encourages connectivity through a random walk objective, using a parameterized model for efficient collective explanation. Furthermore, RAW-Explainer overcomes the distribution shift issue when evaluating explanatory subgraphs that are orders of magnitude smaller than the full graph by proposing a robust evaluator that generalizes to the subgraph distribution. Extensive results on standard knowledge graph completion benchmarks demonstrate that our approach strikes a balance between explanation quality and computational efficiency. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/colab-nyuad/RAWExplainer

entry.title: Rao-Blackwellized e-variables

link.title: Rao-Blackwellized e-variables

entry.content:
We show that for any concave utility, the expected utility of an e-variable can only increase after conditioning on a sufficient statistic, echoing the classic Rao-Blackwell theorem. The simplest form of the result has a straightforward proof using Jensen’s inequality, but we prove more sophisticated versions. We provide several applications of this insight, including a derivation of the log-optimal e-variable for testing the variance in a linear regression model.

entry.title: Regime-Conditioned Evaluation in Multi-Context Bayesian Optimization

link.title: Regime-Conditioned Evaluation in Multi-Context Bayesian Optimization

entry.content:
Published transfer-BO comparisons often estimate an average treatment effect of acquisition choice over hidden regime variables, while practitioners need the conditional effect for their specific prior quality, budget ratio, and metric. An audit of 40 transfer-BO papers from NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AISTATS, UAI, TMLR, JMLR, and AutoML-Conf (2022-2025) finds that 98% never vary B/ A as a controlled axis. On the same GDSC2 benchmark, changing only the budget reverses the ranking: at B=50, Greedy outperforms UCB by 0.050 Hit@1, while at B=100, UCB outperforms Greedy by 0.035. We capture this transition with the Portable Regime Score PRS=(B/ A )(1-rho), where rho is the prior rank correlation and can be estimated from pilot contexts before the main comparison. Across 79 conditions spanning chemistry, drug-response biology, and HPO, a hierarchical model gives beta=0.50 (p=1.1e-9), and 19% of conditions fall in an equivalence zone where advantage <0.01 Hit@1. In five published reversal cases, PRS predicts the winner from pre-comparison observables. A No-Free-Leaderboard proposition explains why unconditional rankings are unstable: when CATE changes sign across regimes, the reported ATE becomes a function of benchmark mixture. RegimePlanner, which estimates rho online and switches acquisition accordingly, wins all 16 HPO-B search spaces at B=100 and exceeds the matched {Greedy,UCB} per-context oracle on GDSC2 by 18%. Pre-registered predictions achieve 27/40=67.5% overall accuracy and above 90% within EMA prior families. The practical protocol is simple: report B/ A , rho, K, and metric alongside any claimed acquisition advantage.

entry.title: Reinforcement Learning in MDPs with Information-Ordered Policies

link.title: Reinforcement Learning in MDPs with Information-Ordered Policies

entry.content:
Many operational Markov decision processes provide structured information where a trajectory generated under one policy may also reveal how other policies would have performed. We formalize this through an information order over a parameterized policy class, writing $\pi_{\theta’} \preceq \pi_\theta$ when data collected under $\pi_\theta$ can be used to estimate the long-run average cost of $\pi_{\theta’}$. We develop an epoch-based reinforcement learning algorithm for infinite-horizon average-cost MDPs with continuous state and action spaces that exploits this order through counterfactual inference. For a $d$-dimensional policy class whose information order has width $w$, the algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{wdT/\alpha})$ regret relative to the optimal policy in the class, where $H$ is a bias span upper bound and $\alpha$ denotes an “information ratio”. Thus, the width captures the effective exploration complexity of the problem, interpolating between full counterfactual feedback and unstructured policy learning. We instantiate the framework in lost-sales inventory systems with positive lead times, dual-sourcing systems governed by dual-index policies, and queues with state-dependent service rates. These applications yield new regret guarantees without requiring global convexity of the average-cost function or specialized arrival-rate structure. Numerical experiments show that exploiting the information order substantially improves learning performance over existing general-purpose and problem-specific benchmarks.

entry.title: Reliable data clustering with Bayesian community detection

link.title: Reliable data clustering with Bayesian community detection

entry.content:
From neuroscience and genomics to systems biology and ecology, researchers rely on clustering similarity data to uncover modular structure. Most methods work in two steps: first reduce noise, then cluster. The first step runs without regard to the second: it forces arbitrary choices, discards useful information, and can impose structure where none exists. Here we bring the two steps together. Using established Bayesian community detection methods, we let one minimum description length criterion choose both how much to sparsify the data and how to cluster it. This one-step approach keeps all the samples for inference, removes the arbitrary threshold choice, and returns a single cluster when there is no real structure. On synthetic data, our approach recovers clusters under more noise and with fewer samples than standard methods. On gene co-expression data from the human brain, it finds more coherent and more stable clusters than WGCNA, the standard tool in the field. Uniting sparsification and clustering in a single model-selection step provides a principled, noise-resistant way to uncover modular structure in similarity data across fields.

entry.title: Robust Estimation under Spurious Correlation via Statistical Counterfactual Augmentation

link.title: Robust Estimation under Spurious Correlation via Statistical Counterfactual Augmentation

entry.content:
Spurious correlations between nuisance features and outcomes present a fundamental challenge for statistical learning and inference. Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), the practice of resampling nuisance features while preserving features of interest, has emerged as a popular strategy to mitigate such correlations, yet its statistical properties, and its reliance on an untestable validity assumption, remain largely unexplored. We provide a statistical treatment of CDA, termed Statistical CDA (SCDA), with two components. First, casting SCDA as a simulated-moment M-estimator, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality with a sandwich covariance and a finite-augmentation-draw variance correction, oracle efficiency for the target parameter, and the equivalence of iterative and one-shot procedures via stochastic approximation, yielding valid large-sample inference where previously none was available. Second, because the augmentation’s validity cannot be tested from the observed data when features are entangled (a fact we prove), we develop a sensitivity analysis that bounds the residual nuisance–outcome dependence by a parameter $\Gamma$, giving sharp identified intervals for the target with valid confidence intervals and a breakdown frontier; the point-identified theory is the $\Gamma=0$ special case. Simulations confirm the efficiency gains under validity and the robustness bounds under possible invalidity, placing a widely used augmentation method on a transparent inferential footing.

entry.title: Robust Experimental Design via Generalised Bayesian Inference

link.title: Robust Experimental Design via Generalised Bayesian Inference

entry.content:
Bayesian optimal experimental design is a principled framework for conducting experiments that leverages Bayesian inference to quantify how much information one can expect to gain from selecting a certain design. However, accurate Bayesian inference relies on the assumption that one’s statistical model of the data-generating process is correctly specified. If this assumption is violated, Bayesian methods can lead to poor inference and estimates of information gain. Generalised Bayesian (or Gibbs) inference is a more robust probabilistic inference framework that replaces the likelihood in the Bayesian update by a suitable loss function. In this work, we present Generalised Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (GBOED), an extension of generalised Bayesian inference to the experimental design setting which achieves robustness in both design and inference. Using a generalisation of Bayesian decision theory, we derive a new acquisition function, the Gibbs expected information gain. Our empirical results demonstrate that GBOED can enhance robustness to outliers and incorrect assumptions about the outcome noise distribution.

entry.title: Robust Local Fréchet Regression: Nonasymptotic Theory and Minimax Optimality

link.title: Robust Local Fréchet Regression: Nonasymptotic Theory and Minimax Optimality

entry.content:
We develop robust local Fr'echet regression for heavy-tailed responses in a general metric space and propose a distance-based median-of-means estimator. We derive nonasymptotic pointwise high-probability bounds separately under local second-order smoothness and local $1$-Wasserstein H"older continuity, and show that the corresponding optimized rates match the classical pointwise rates for nonparametric regression. We also establish matching pointwise minimax lower bounds over embedded Gaussian regression subclasses. Remarkably, our results do not require an entropy condition on the response space. Simulation studies with positive-definite matrix-valued responses, together with a real-data application involving Wasserstein-valued responses, illustrate the robustness–efficiency tradeoff and practical performance of the proposed estimator.

entry.title: SLIM: Stochastic Learning and Inference in Nonlinear GMM Models

link.title: SLIM: Stochastic Learning and Inference in Nonlinear GMM Models

entry.content:
We propose SLIM (Stochastic Learning and Inference in overidentified Models), a new scalable stochastic approximation algorithm for nonlinear GMMs with many nonseparable moments and parameters. SLIM is shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal without a consistent initial estimator or a globally convex GMM criterion. Random-scaling and plug-in based confidence set constructions remain valid when computational uncertainty can be non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. An optional second-order refinement achieves full-sample GMM efficiency. We develop $J$-tests for SLIM. The theoretical results are extended to models with clustered data of unequal cluster sizes. Monte Carlo experiments for a nonlinear demand system with 576 moments and 380 parameters demonstrate computational gains and scalability to one million observations. A LinkedIn application with 4.8 million college graduates illustrates clustered estimation and inference for first employment destinations.

entry.title: Scaling Spatially Varying Distributed Lag Nonlinear Models for Nationwide Small-Area Data: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach

link.title: Scaling Spatially Varying Distributed Lag Nonlinear Models for Nationwide Small-Area Data: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach

entry.content:
Lagged and nonlinear exposure-response relationships are frequently modelled using distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs). However, these relationships can vary substantially across locations due to differences in climate, population structure, adaptation and socio-economic characteristics, among others. Spatially-varying DLNMs can capture this heterogeneity, but their computational demands limit their application to fine-scale nationwide datasets with thousands of small areas. In this paper, we adapt a ‘divide-and-conquer’ approach to spatially varying DLNMs. The method partitions the spatial domain into smaller regions, expands each region with a k-order neighbourhood to reduce boundary effects, fits separate models within each partition using Laplacian P-splines, and combines the resulting estimates using conditional predictive ordinate-based mixture weights. We evaluated the approach in a simulation study based on municipalities in Sicily and applied it to daily summer temperature and mortality data from 7122 municipalities in mainland Italy between 2011 and 2021. Simulation studies show good performance, with relative-risk estimates comparable to those from a global model and relatively robust to the choice and number of partitioning units. Computational efficiency can be substantially improved by using parallel computations. The Italian application reveals significant spatial heterogeneity in the temperature-mortality relationship, with clear regional differences. The proposed framework makes spatially varying DLNMs feasible for large, fine-scale spatiotemporal datasets while retaining location-specific exposure-lag-response estimation.

entry.title: Sharp Instrumental Variable Bounds under The Marginal Sensitivity Model

link.title: Sharp Instrumental Variable Bounds under The Marginal Sensitivity Model

entry.content:
Marginal sensitivity models bound the degree of unmeasured confounding but do not incorporate instrumental-variable restrictions, even when an instrument is available. We develop a framework combining these models with instrumental-variable assumptions to sharpen inference on population treatment effects without requiring treatment monotonicity or treatment-effect homogeneity. For continuous and finite ordered outcomes, we characterize sharp identified sets for potential-outcome means and the average treatment effect, together with observable restrictions implied jointly by the instrumental-variable and sensitivity assumptions. The bounds admit explicit formulas for finite ordered outcomes, while optimization over prespecified threshold classes provides tractable outer bounds for continuous outcomes. We develop cross-fitted one-step estimators that accommodate flexible nuisance estimation. Under suitable conditions, the resulting outward confidence sets asymptotically cover the sharp identified interval without requiring optimal threshold estimation. Stronger conditions yield semiparametric efficient estimation and inference for restricted-class bounds. Numerical experiments show narrower confidence sets when incorporating an instrument and compare the performance of outward inference and inference for individual bounds. We apply the framework to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment to illustrate how combining instrumental-variable assumptions with restrictions on the degree of unmeasured confounding can strengthen conclusions about the effect of Medicaid coverage on emergency-department use.

entry.title: Source-Aware Dynamic Pricing with Strategic Buyers

link.title: Source-Aware Dynamic Pricing with Strategic Buyers

entry.content:
In modern commerce, firms and platforms typically use customer features from different sources to personalize prices: some features are verified using seller records or third-party data, while others are self-reported and may be strategically manipulated by buyers seeking lower prices. We therefore introduce a novel source-aware framework for contextual dynamic pricing with strategic buyers in a high-dimensional semiparametric setting, where buyer valuations follow a sparse linear model with an unknown noise distribution. To account for differences in manipulability across feature sources while enabling effective valuation learning, we develop the Source-Aware Localized exploration and calibrated Exploitation (SALE) pricing policy, which draws on verified features to localize price exploration and combines verified and reported features to correct for strategic manipulation during exploitation. Our localized exploration design allows converting binary purchase feedback into unbiased signals of conditional mean valuations, yielding a new population equation that supports consistent sparse estimation despite non-i.i.d. buyer arrivals. Building on this estimate, we develop a localized empirical-process analysis that exploits intrinsic sparse geometry to establish uniform guarantees for nonparametric estimation of the noise distribution in the high-dimensional setting. With these estimation guarantees, we establish SALE’s self-recovery property, which keeps localized exploration valid with high probability and leads to a sublinear expected regret bound. Both simulation studies and real-data experiments demonstrate the appealing performance of SALE. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to provide a theoretical and practical framework for incorporating information provenance into dynamic pricing with strategic buyers.

entry.title: Sparsity-Corrected Tensor Clustering for Multi-Layer Networks

link.title: Sparsity-Corrected Tensor Clustering for Multi-Layer Networks

entry.content:
Multi-layer networks provide complementary views of interactions among the same set of nodes. In practice, layers with similar community structures may have substantially different network sparsity, causing sparsity variation to obscure the structural patterns of interest. To address this problem, a sparsity heterogeneous mixture multi-layer stochastic block model is proposed, which separates layer-specific sparsity from group-specific community structure. Based on the induced low-rank tensor representation, a sparsity-corrected tensor clustering method is proposed to remove the layer-specific scale effect before clustering, without explicitly estimating the sparsity parameters. Theoretical guarantees for tensor decomposition, layer clustering, and community detection are established. The results further characterize the range of sparsity heterogeneity allowed for consistent recovery, including regimes where the sparsity ratio diverges with the network dimensions. Numerical studies and an application to international trade networks from BACI demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under heterogeneous layer sparsity.

entry.title: Spectral Indistinguishability and Learning-Curve Identifiability in Quadratic Networks

link.title: Spectral Indistinguishability and Learning-Curve Identifiability in Quadratic Networks

entry.content:
Motivated by information-organization sculpting, we study spectral summaries and scalar learning curves in centered quadratic networks. We construct analytic positive input densities with Gaussian one- and two-coordinate marginals. Their complete fourth-moment operators are orthogonally intertwined by a map fixing the entire diagonal teacher algebra, giving equal anchored spectral measures. For selected common teachers with a nonzero cycle invariant, their factorized loss curves differ because the map does not preserve matrix multiplication. Cycle length $r$, which can be arbitrarily large, gives $O(\varepsilon^r)$ contrast uniformly in training time for each fixed construction. For a supplied pair, noisy scalar loss queries require order $\varepsilon^{-2r}$ observations, while bounded initialization interventions with scalar gradient readouts require order $\varepsilon^{-2}$. A shared-input score, equal to a paired-gradient difference, attains the optimal input-sample exponent without knowing the teacher. An explicit family of diverging auxiliary teacher scales instead admits a nonzero finite limiting contrast at coupling $1/\log L$. Conversely, for Gaussian inputs and a rationally independent teacher spectrum, one exact scalar loss curve identifies the initial predictor up to sign conjugation. Within this rationally independent class, with nonzero diagonal inverse-state error in every coordinate and calibrated time and loss scales, it also identifies the unknown teacher spectrum and active dimension, modulo simultaneous rotations. entry.title: Stabilizing Thompson Sampling with Null Hypothesis Bayesian Response-Adaptive Randomization

link.title: Stabilizing Thompson Sampling with Null Hypothesis Bayesian Response-Adaptive Randomization

entry.content:
Response-adaptive randomization (RAR) methods can be used to adapt randomization probabilities based on accumulating data, aiming to increase the probability of allocating patients to effective treatments. A popular RAR method is Thompson sampling, which randomizes patients proportionally to the Bayesian posterior probability that each treatment is the most effective. However, its high variability can also increase the risk of assigning patients to inferior treatments and lead to inferential problems such as confidence interval undercoverage. We propose a principled method based on Bayesian hypothesis testing to address these issues: We introduce a null hypothesis postulating equal effectiveness of treatments. Bayesian model averaging then induces shrinkage toward equal randomization probabilities, with the degree of shrinkage controlled by the prior probability of the null hypothesis. Equal randomization and Thompson sampling arise as special cases when the prior probability is one or zero, respectively. A simulation study demonstrates that the method can mitigate issues with Thompson sampling and has comparable statistical properties to Thompson sampling with common ad hoc modifications such as power transformation and probability capping. Under the null hypothesis and a normal model, the randomization probabilities are shown to converge asymptotically to equal randomization, unlike those of Thompson sampling. We implement the method in the free and open-source R package brar, enabling experimenters to easily perform null hypothesis Bayesian RAR and support more effective randomization of patients.

entry.title: Structural Causal Bottleneck Models

link.title: Structural Causal Bottleneck Models

entry.content:
We introduce structural causal bottleneck models (SCBMs), a novel class of structural causal models in which causal effects between high-dimensional variables are mediated by low-dimensional summary statistics, or bottlenecks. SCBMs provide a flexible framework for mechanism-specific, target-dependent dimension reduction while remaining estimable via standard learning algorithms. We prove that bottleneck variables are identifiable up to bijection from observational data, and validate this experimentally. We then study causal effect estimation in linear SCBMs under three standard adjustment strategies. For instrumental variables, we identify a population-level non-identifiability of na"ive two-stage least squares when all variables are high-dimensional, and show that bottleneck representations restore identification. For mediation and backdoor adjustment, we prove that conditioning on bottleneck variables yields valid effect estimates with explicit finite-sample efficiency gains over conditioning on full high-dimensional variables. We argue that SCBMs provide a principled alternative to existing causal dimension reduction frameworks such as causal representation learning and causal abstractions.

entry.title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy

link.title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy

entry.content:
R`enyi differential privacy, based on R`enyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, R`enyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, R`enyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in R`enyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for R`enyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.

entry.title: Testing Treatment Effect Heterogeneity with Functional Outcomes

link.title: Testing Treatment Effect Heterogeneity with Functional Outcomes

entry.content:
Assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity is important in causal inference, particularly for functional outcomes where effects may vary over time and the common effect is unknown. We propose a nonparametric procedure that assesses treatment-effect homogeneity through a testable marginal implication. By comparing within-arm difference distributions, the construction removes the unknown common functional effect without estimating it. We measure departures between these distributions through an integrated squared discrepancy of their characteristic functionals. A full-support Gaussian integrating measure yields an explicit bounded-kernel representation and identifies equality of the difference laws without requiring moment conditions on the outcomes. We construct an unbiased generalized U-statistic that accounts for dependence among overlapping differences, derive its null, fixed-alternative, and local-alternative limits, and develop a centered multiplier bootstrap for inference. The framework extends to multiple treatment arms with a shared control. For computation, a random-direction approximation combined with a nine-state recursion reduces the cost to linear order in the sample size for fixed numerical settings. Simulation studies assess the finite-sample performance of the proposed procedure relative to several benchmark methods. An application to the Irish gas smart-metering trial illustrates its use for assessing heterogeneity in functional treatment responses.

entry.title: Testing the equality of parameters in fixed and increasing dimension

link.title: Testing the equality of parameters in fixed and increasing dimension

entry.content:
This paper proposes a general and unified framework for testing the equality of a broad class of parameters, defined as a smooth function of expectations of symmetric kernels, across multiple independent populations. We consider two test statistics, a Wald-type statistic and an ANOVA-type statistic. The asymptotic distribution of the first one is derived under a fixed-dimension regime, whereas the second one is studied under both fixed and increasing-dimension regimes, where the parameter dimension diverges with the sample size. Based on these limiting distributions, we construct test procedures enabling asymptotically exact inference without parametric assumptions. Additionally, an alternative null distribution estimator based on a weighted bootstrap approximation is studied, which is applicable to the ANOVA-type statistic under a fixed-dimension regime. The finite-sample performance and computational efficiency of the proposed procedures are evaluated through an extensive simulation study and a real dataset application.

entry.title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks

link.title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks

entry.content:
Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. Corresponding deep learning methods are developed as bundles: a new architecture together with a new training loss, tested on one to five datasets against a handful of baselines. Thus, a state-of-the-art result cannot be attributed to the architecture, the loss, or the evaluation protocol. The coupling is not accidental: with one incidence curve per cause, a network’s head is tied to the losses expressible on it. We vary the two axes independently, three losses, two of them strictly proper, on four backbones, across two modalities that tease the axes apart: 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. One loss wins in both: modelling cumulative incidence directly under censoring weighting. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. This is an avenue of progress: composed, the two give a model nobody has tried, RealMLP or TabM trained with the cumulative-incidence loss, which takes the best Brier score in our benchmark.

entry.title: The Statistical Fairness-Accuracy Frontier

link.title: The Statistical Fairness-Accuracy Frontier

entry.content:
We study fairness-accuracy tradeoffs when a single predictive model must serve multiple demographic groups. A useful tool for understanding this tradeoff is the fairness-accuracy (FA) Pareto frontier, which characterizes the set of models that cannot be improved in either fairness or accuracy without worsening the other. While characterizing the FA frontier requires full knowledge of the data distribution, we focus on the finite-sample regime, quantifying how well a designer can approximate any point on the frontier from limited data and bounding the worst-case gap. In particular, we derive worst-case-optimal estimators that depend on the designer’s knowledge of the covariate distribution. For each estimator, we characterize how finite-sample effects asymmetrically impact each group’s welfare and identify optimal sample allocation strategies. Finally, we provide uniform finite-sample bounds along the entire FA frontier, quantifying finite-sample deviations across alternative fairness-accuracy tradeoffs.

entry.title: The kinematics of global warming: Semiparametric analysis of warming level, rate, and acceleration

link.title: The kinematics of global warming: Semiparametric analysis of warming level, rate, and acceleration

entry.content:
We develop a semiparametric kinematic state-space framework for estimating the latent dynamics of global warming from noisy monthly temperature observations. The framework estimates the warming level, warming rate, and warming acceleration jointly, while incorporating covariates, measurement error, serial dependence, and time-varying error variance directly in the model. Applying the framework to five major global temperature records, and comparing it with nonparametric kernel and parametric benchmark estimators, we show that the inferred recent warming dynamics depend crucially on the parametric restrictions imposed on the warming path. The current underlying warming level is robustly estimated across datasets and methods, with estimates close to (1.40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}) above pre-industrial levels. Estimates of the current warming rate differ materially across estimator classes: flexible local estimators imply substantially higher current rates than the parametric benchmarks. Our preferred state-space specification estimates the current warming rate at approximately (0.47\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \, \textnormal{decade}^{-1}). Endpoint acceleration estimates from the flexible estimators are positive across all five records, although their statistical significance varies across records and methods. Average acceleration since 2015 is significantly positive across all five records in the preferred state-space model, with a cross-dataset mean of approximately (0.19\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \, \textnormal{decade}^{-2}). Our results indicate that global warming is proceeding faster, and has accelerated more strongly in the recent period, than conventional estimates suggest.

link.title: The optimal information complexity of VC learning

entry.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes

link.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes

entry.content:
When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable’s entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens. A reanalyzed credit-scoring study shows the cost: a characteristic an optimizing selector uses cannot satisfy exclusion.

entry.title: Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model

link.title: Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model

entry.content:
Nonstationarity and heterogeneous dynamics are common in financial and macroeconomic time series. Volatility alternates between calm and turbulent regimes, interest rates follow monetary-policy cycles, and major events trigger persistent structural shifts. We propose the Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model (TPGPMM), a Bayesian nonparametric framework for regime identification and nonstationary prediction that infers such regimes and their within-regime dependence from data, without Markovian assumptions. It combines (i) an adaptive Pitman-Yor process prior on ordered compositions, mapped to block lengths with contiguity enforced by construction, and (ii) regime-specific Gaussian processes for temporal dependence, yielding a nonstationary predictive distribution. By inferring its discount parameter, the prior adapts to homogeneous and highly heterogeneous regime lengths. Unlike sequential or Markov-switching methods, it flags persistent structural shifts as change points rather than reacting to transient shocks. A split-merge Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with exact Gibbs updates of regime boundaries jointly learns change points and hyperparameters in batch, quantifying uncertainty over the partition and within-regime dynamics. With an RBF kernel and a fixed, data-informed noise level, TPGPMM produces a sparse, confident segmentation. On simulated data it recovers the true regimes, and on the CBOE Volatility Index and the 10-year US Treasury yield it identifies regimes aligned with documented market and monetary-policy events. For prediction, variants estimating the noise level fit better than change-point baselines and fit and forecast better than the main specification, at the cost of a less sparse or less event-aligned segmentation; with a regime mean, they fit better than a fitted stationary Gaussian process and have lower forecast RMSE except at the shortest horizons.

entry.title: Token-Level Attribution of Multi-Mode LLM Watermarks: Optimal Rule and Belief Weighting

link.title: Token-Level Attribution of Multi-Mode LLM Watermarks: Optimal Rule and Belief Weighting

entry.content:
A watermark verifier may hold many modes, i.e., secret keys, and a document may mix spans of different modes with unwatermarked text. Directly reporting the mode with the largest pivotal statistic (pivot) inflates the Type I error, and restoring the nominal level reduces power as candidate modes are added. We formulate token-level multi-mode attribution for the Gumbel-max watermark as maximizing correct-label power under a Type I error constraint given a mode prior. We show that the optimal rule reports the mode with the largest prior-weighted alternative density and rejects when this density exceeds one common threshold. Based on this rule, we propose the Belief-weighted Likelihood Attribution with Density Estimation (BLADE) detector. It estimates the mode prior from neighboring pivots and the alternative density from reference token probabilities. Under a conditional product model of the pivots, it keeps the exact Type I error. We further show that BLADE approaches the optimal rule as its prior and density estimates improve, with a sharp coefficient on the density error. On OPT-1.3B and other open-weight large language models, BLADE attains higher correct-label power than the compared detectors across candidate counts, token-substitution rates, generation temperatures and generator models.

link.title: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization

entry.content:
Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. entry.title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning

link.title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning

entry.content:
We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost $\Delta$. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.

entry.title: Unit-level aggregation breaks coverage in causal foundation models

link.title: Unit-level aggregation breaks coverage in causal foundation models

entry.content:
Causal foundation models (CFMs) show promising results for treatment-effect estimation, with unit-level estimates that are competitive on standard benchmarks. Many causal analyses, however, inform decisions through effects averaged over groups of units, such as the full sample, the treated units, or a subgroup, and for such decisions a CFM is useful only if its credible intervals are calibrated. We examine these intervals and find that their coverage degrades, both in simple synthetic settings and on standard benchmarks. On ACIC 2016, for example, temperature-calibrated 95% intervals from CausalPFN fall below nominal coverage beyond groups of 30 out of 4802 units, and intervals for the full-sample average contain the true value in only 20% of datasets. We trace this problem to how these models are trained and how their intervals are formed. They output a predictive distribution for one unit at a time and, at inference time, combine the unit-level variances as if the errors on different units were independent. We show formally that posterior uncertainty over the data-generating process makes these errors correlated. As a result, the combined variance is too small by a factor that grows with the size of the group. Empirically, this factor predicts where coverage fails and by how much. We then show that two neural process models, which make joint predictions for a group of units, account for this correlation and substantially improve coverage on synthetic tasks and, as heads on a frozen CausalPFN, on all six benchmarks.

entry.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks

link.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks

entry.content:
The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.

entry.title: Weighted spatial averages with missing observations: Convergence and accuracy of delta-method variance approximations

link.title: Weighted spatial averages with missing observations: Convergence and accuracy of delta-method variance approximations

entry.content:
Weighted spatial averages from incomplete networks are ratios whose variance is approximated by truncating a Taylor series (the delta method). Three questions remain open: whether the series converges, how large a truncation’s error is, and how it behaves as the network grows. We address these for observations missing completely at random, independently with a common probability $\alpha$. First, the truncations, which count corrections for the denominator (the total reported weight) and for its coupling with the numerator, converge for a given network only if $\alpha>\tfrac12$ and both corrections increase together. Second, whether or not the series converges, the error of truncations correcting only for the denominator is controlled at any network size by its coefficient of variation $\rho$, with $\rho^2=\tfrac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\sum_i\beta_i^2$ for weights $\beta_i$, and by the probability of rare reporting patterns. Third, for uniform weights and bounded fields, these errors vanish as the network grows, at any fixed availability. If correlations also decay with distance, the first-order approximation of earlier work has error of order $\rho^4$, against $\rho^2$ for the simplest approximation. Only truncations of equal order in numerator and denominator, beginning with the first-order truncation, avoid spurious dependence on the mean level; higher ones need not be more accurate. The exact variance for uniform weights, a single sum, shows that for correlated fields the first-order approximation overstates the contribution of missing data but is conservative overall. Concentrated weights degrade it more than $\rho$ indicates. Rainfall simulations over India illustrates results, several of which extend to self-normalized estimators.

entry.title: What is causal about causal models and representations?

link.title: What is causal about causal models and representations?

entry.content:
Causal Bayesian networks are often described as causal because they support reasoning about interventions. Yet interventions are defined in the mathematical model, whereas the resulting model predictions concern the effects of actions in the real world. Consequently, whether and how a causal model makes falsifiable predictions about the effects of actions depends on how actions are interpreted as interventions. This requires specifying which actions correspond to which interventions, a step that is frequently left implicit. We develop a formal framework that separates a causal model from the data-generating process it aims to describe and formalizes interpretations connecting actions to interventions. Within this framework, we prove an impossibility result: no interpretation can simultaneously satisfy a collection of desirable properties while remaining non-circular. Under a circular interpretation, every model that fits the observational distribution is interventionally valid, so no experiment can falsify it. We analyze several non-circular alternatives and discuss implications for falsification, causal discovery, causal representation learning, and causal abstraction. More broadly, our framework provides a way to make assumptions about the connections between actions and interventions explicit and to reason formally about the empirical content of causal models.
